content_list.content_text: Australian cinema in the 1970s and early 1980s was an industry sharply divided in two. On one side, the prestige productions of Fred Schepisi (b. 1939), Peter Weir (b. 1944) and Gillian Armstrong (b. 1950) told quintessentially Australian stories: elaborate, lovingly crafted, rich in artistic integrity and quiet grace.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Cars That Ate Paris
information.contentText: Peter Weir came up with the idea for the film while driving through Europe, where signs on the main French roads diverted him into what he saw as strange little villages. It originally started as a comedy to star Grahame Bond, but later evolved. Piers Davies and Keith Gow also contributed. He then took the film to the McElroy brothers, who had already worked in a wide variety of positions on several films. Most of the budget came from the Australian Film Development Corporation, with additional funding from Royce Smeal Film Productions in Sydney.

content_list.content_text: On the other side, the booming B-movie industry offered a parade of crude sex comedies, punch-heavy action-adventure films and inventive gory horror films, collectively known as Ozploitation.

content_list.title: Ozploitation
content_list.description:
"Ozploitation" films are a type of horror, comedy and action film, usually low-budget, made in Australia after the introduction of the R rating in 1971.

Ozploitation is often considered a minor wave within the Australian New Wave. ("At a time when neck-breaking action, B-grade horror, comedy and 'fun' vulgar sex came together in a new wave of cinema"). Several directors "ventured" heavily into the genre, among them Brian Trenchard-Smith, David Hemmings, Tony Williams, Greg McLean, John V. Soto, Tim Burstall, Sandy Harbutt, Richard Franklin, and George Miller, who made his name with the "Mad Max" trilogy (after a long time in development, in 2015, 30 years after the last film was released, the fourth film in the series, "Fury Road," came out).

The origin of the term is credited to the documentary Not Quite Hollywood: The Wild, Untold Story of Ozploitation! (2008).
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Ozploitation" on Wikipedia.

content_list.content_text: In the late 1960s, aside from a few historical dramas, in many cases financed from abroad, the Australian film industry had created very few productions of its own. In the early 1970s, however, a confluence of events changed that picture. A new artistic counterculture emerged; the increasingly popular national television industry trained directors, actors and producers; and a series of government initiatives and tax incentives made filmmaking a far more attractive business. The result was the country's creative wave in cinema, dubbed the "Australian New Wave" by the press.

information.contentText: A number of small changes were made to the film for its U.S. release, where it was distributed theatrically by Paramount Pictures in September 1986. There are two versions of the film: the Australian version and an international version, in which much of the Australian slang was replaced with more commonly understood terms, and which has a shorter running time. It grossed US$174,803,506 at the U.S. box office.

content_list.content_text: The first hits were ocker comedies (a term used for crude, uncultivated Australians), films about suburban life and sexual frustration that reflected the new cultural freedom while both celebrating and mocking Australian notions of masculinity and culture.

quote.quote: I'm scared, Fifi... Look, any longer out on that road and I'm one of them, a terminal crazy...
quote.author: Max Rockatansky (Mel Gibson) in Mad Max

content_list.content_text: Curiously, the most important figure of the period, Peter Weir (b. 1944), began his career with a work that fit neither B-movie production nor the prestige group: The Cars That Ate Paris (1974) is an exploitation film, but one that shows neither sex nor gore, with clear influences from European art cinema.

information.contentText: The film initially received a polarized reception upon its release in April 1979, although it won four AACTA Awards and attracted a following, and its critical reputation has grown since. Shot on a budget of $400,000, it grossed more than US$100 million worldwide and held the Guinness record for most profitable film. The success of Mad Max has been credited with further opening the global market to Australian New Wave films.

content_list.content_text: His next film, Picnic at Hanging Rock (1975), however, came to define everything that quality Australian cinema stood for: stunning landscapes, carefully reconstructed period settings, beauty, silence and a sense of something terrible lurking. The film both celebrates and questions aspects of Australian culture, specifically the powerful influence of the British, the quiet reliance on a class system, and an Aboriginal culture trampled by colonialism.

Taking their cue from Picnic at Hanging Rock, Australia's prestige filmmakers used cinema to revisit aspects of the country's colonial past. The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith (1978) evoked the savagery of the nation's birth, portraying the colonial forces as murderous thugs waging a war for dominance and crushing the native population in their path. Meanwhile, Gillian Armstrong's (b. 1950) My Brilliant Career (1979) and Weir's Gallipoli (1981) explored the country's attempts to survive the decline of the British Empire.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Picnic at Hanging Rock
information.contentText: Works of Australian Impressionism, such as Frederick McCubbin's Lost (1886), inspired the film's themes and visual style.

content_list.content_text: B-movie production was also finding its footing. The biker film Stone (1974) took the template of Roger Corman's epic motorcycle-rebel movies and added explicit sex, violence and a shrewd awareness of Australian identity, paving the way for the country's biggest hit, Mad Max (1979), a worldwide success. The latter introduced a new international star: Mel Gibson (b. 1956) had the looks and swagger of a classic movie icon, but with an added toughness and emotional instability. His hugely successful decision to leave Australia for Hollywood set a precedent for countless actors and directors.

content_list.title: Mad Max: The New Australian Cinema Goes Global
content_list.description:
Although its sequel usually gets most of the critical praise, it all began with the striking Mad Max, released two years earlier. It was here that Miller first brought to the screen his hellish vision of an inhospitable, gang-ruled Australia, with the help of a newcomer actor named Mel Gibson.

Gibson was only 23 when he landed the role of Max Rockatansky (legend has it that Gibson auditioned for the part the day after getting into a bar fight, and his bruised face stuck in the casting director's mind). Gibson was so unknown that when Mad Max was about to be released in the United States, he didn't even appear in the trailers, which showed only explosions and car crashes. In hindsight, of course, the leather-jacketed antihero Gibson created is a fundamental element of the film.

In a decaying, futuristic Australia, Rockatansky is a motorcycle cop trying to keep order in a rapidly disintegrating society. Gangs roam the abandoned highways, raping and robbing at will, and one of these groups ends up at the house where Max's wife and child are staying. When they are murdered, Max seeks revenge and unleashes a wave of violence involving spectacular car chases, brutal fights and nonstop action.

Most impressive is the fact that the whole film cost just 400,000 dollars, a budget so tight that Miller reportedly had to wreck his own car for one scene. In the end, though, it grossed more than 100 million dollars, making it one of the most profitable films of all time. Mad Max deservedly became a cult hit around the world (curiously, it was dubbed into "American English" in the United States because it was thought audiences wouldn't understand the Australian accent) and remains a memorable film to this day.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Joanna Berry, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Australian B movies often outdid their better-funded American counterparts. The work of American-born screenwriter Everett De Roche, in films such as the eco-satire Long Weekend (1978), fused the typical thrills of a low-budget B movie with smart dialogue and sharp ideas about psychology, ecology and landscape, filtered through an outsider's affectionate perspective on his adopted country.

information.contentText: My Brilliant Career has been noted by film historians as part of the Australian New Wave. In a retrospective essay celebrating the film's inclusion in the Criterion Collection, film scholar Carrie Rickey notes that both the film and its source novel "have become part of the Australian identity."
information.source: YouTube: National Film and Sound Archive of Australia (NFSA) channel

content_list.content_text: Both the prestige strand and the B-movie strand began to falter in the mid-1980s, as government funding shrank and many leading directors, such as Peter Weir, headed for Hollywood. (Fred Schepisi was so disillusioned by the poor reception of The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith at home that he left Australia and took 10 years to shoot there again.)

Australian film culture today is little different from that of any small Western country: it produces a large number of modest dramas, a steady stream of talented screenwriters, actors and directors with their eyes on Hollywood, and the occasional worldwide hit such as Crocodile Dundee (1986). Starring and written by comedian Paul Hogan (b. 1939), that film (and its sequels) was initially aimed at the large American audience, but managed to win over international audiences. Although it seems unlikely that filmmakers will recapture the spirit of daring and experimentation that defined the 1970s and 1980s, Australian cinema remains synonymous with popular, intelligent and well-made films.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Tom Huddleston, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: Mad Max
movies.overview: Taking place in a dystopian Australia in the near future, Mad Max tells the story of a highway patrolman cruising the squalid back roads that have become the breeding ground of criminals foraging for gasoline and scraps. After some grisly events at the hands of a motorcycle gang, Max sets out across the barren wastelands in search of revenge.

movies.title: Crocodile Dundee
movies.overview: When a New York reporter plucks crocodile hunter Dundee from the Australian Outback for a visit to the Big Apple, it's a clash of cultures and a recipe for good-natured comedy as naïve Dundee negotiates the concrete jungle. Dundee proves that his instincts are quite useful in the city and adeptly handles everything from wily muggers to high-society snoots without breaking a sweat.

movies.title: Picnic at Hanging Rock
movies.overview: In the early 1900s, Miranda attends a girls boarding school in Australia. One Valentine's Day, the school's typically strict headmistress treats the girls to a picnic field trip to an unusual but scenic volcanic formation called Hanging Rock. Despite rules against it, Miranda and several other girls venture off. It's not until the end of the day that the faculty realizes the girls and one of the teachers have disappeared mysteriously.

movies.title: My Brilliant Career
movies.overview: A young woman who is determined to maintain her independence finds herself at odds with her family who wants her to tame her wild side and get married.

movies.title: Walkabout
movies.overview: Under the pretense of having a picnic, a geologist takes his teenage daughter and 6-year-old son into the Australian outback and attempts to shoot them. When he fails, he turns the gun on himself, and the two city-bred children must contend with harsh wilderness alone. They are saved by a chance encounter with an Aborigine boy who shows them how to survive, and in the process underscores the disharmony between nature and modern life.

movies.title: Stork
movies.overview: Stork is a gangly young man, a virgin with an overactive imagination who thinks he’s a revolutionary. Bored with a design job at General Motors Holden in Melbourne, he drops out and moves into a share house with his mate Westy. He daydreams his way through life, bungling job interviews, upsetting ‘respectable’ people, and getting drunk. The only girl in the house, Anna resists Stork’s advances, because she’s already involved with the other two resident males, Tony and Clyde. But when she becomes pregnant and Clyde and Anna decide to marry, Stork, Tony, Clyde and Westy are shocked when they realize that either one of the foursome could be the father. Then the fun begins....

movies.title: The Adventures of Barry McKenzie
movies.overview: Barry McKenzie sets off for England with his aunt, Edna Everage, to advance his cultural education. Bazza is an innocent abroad, fond of beer, Bondi and beautiful sheilas, but he soon settles into the Australian ghetto in Earls Court, where his old mate Curly has a flat.

movies.title: The Cars That Ate Paris
movies.overview: After the death of his brother on the road, unemployed and unstable drifter Arthur Waldo stays for a while in the rural Australian town of Paris as the guest of the mayor, who hopes he will become a permanent member of the Paris population. Arthur soon realizes the quaint hamlet has a sinister secret: they orchestrate car accidents and rob the victims. Survivors are brought to the local hospital, lobotomized, and used for a local doctor's experiments.

movies.title: Sunday Too Far Away
movies.overview: A hard-drinking but hard-working gun shearer leads a group of Outback sheep herders into striking after wealthy landowners attempt to drive them from their territory.

movies.title: Don's Party
movies.overview: Don's Party stars John Hargreaves as Don Henderson, a schoolteacher living with his wife, Kath (Jeanie Drynan), in 1969. Out of boredom, he invites a small group of friends to celebrate a predicted Australian Labor Party (ALP) election victory, much to the dismay of his wife.

movies.title: Newsfront
movies.overview: Surprisingly adventurous saga of an intrepid group of cinematographers and reporters who risk life and limb to capture footage of breaking news for the movie-going public.

movies.title: Patrick
movies.overview: A comatose hospital patient harasses and kills though his powers of telekinesis to claim his private nurse as his own.

movies.title: Gallipoli
movies.overview: As World War I rages, brave and youthful Australians Archy and Frank—both agile runners—become friends and enlist in the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps together. They later find themselves part of the Dardanelles Campaign on the Gallipoli peninsula, a brutal eight-month conflict which pit the British and their allies against the Ottoman Empire and left over 500,000 men dead.

movies.title: Turkey Shoot
movies.overview: In the near future, after an unspecified holocaust, survivors are herded into prison camps. There, they are hunted for sport by the leaders of the camp. Paul, one of the newest prisoners, is determined not to go down as quietly as the others.

movies.title: The Year My Voice Broke
movies.overview: Set in 1962, a young prepubescent boy in rural Australia watches painfully as his best friend and first love blossoms into womanhood and falls for a thuggish rugby player, changing the lives of everyone involved.

content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1970 to 1989
content_list.description: The Exorcist is released, making audiences around the world sick and causing them to faint, creating a global hysteria. The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies.
